title: Backoff lowers load. Jitter breaks synchronization.
topic: How exponential backoff helps manage repeated retry attempts in networks

scenes.title: What is a Retry Storm?
scenes.narration: When many devices or programs try to reconnect to a service right after it fails, they can all send requests at the same time. This sudden surge is called a retry storm. It overwhelms the server and makes it even harder for anyone to connect.

visual.caption: All devices retry simultaneously, causing a high surge of requests.

scenes.title: How Regular Retries Cause Problems
scenes.narration: If every device waits a fixed short time before retrying, they keep hitting the server together. This repeated, synchronized traffic locks up resources and can lead to longer delays or service crashes.

visual.caption: Fixed retry intervals lead to repeated, synchronized retries that worsen server overload.

scenes.title: Introducing Exponential Backoff
scenes.narration: Exponential backoff increases the delay between attempts, often doubling it up to a limit. This reduces each client’s retry frequency and gives the service time to recover. Identical clients can still retry together, so backoff alone does not break synchronization.

visual.formula: Wait time for retry n = 2 to the power of (n - 1) seconds
visual.caption: Illustrative delay ceilings: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds.

scenes.title: Add jitter to spread the requests
scenes.narration: With full jitter, each client samples a random delay between zero and its current backoff ceiling. Independent random delays spread requests across time. Combined with a retry limit and a total timeout, this reduces repeated pressure without promising that every request will succeed.

visual.caption: Jitter breaks synchronized retries. Backoff lowers their frequency.
